notes.definition: The atom economy (atom utilisation) of a reaction is a measure of the amount of starting materials that end up as useful products. It is calculated as the relative formula mass of the desired product divided by the sum of the relative formula masses of all the reactants, as a percentage.
explanation: Most reactions make more than one product. Usually only one of them is wanted: this is the desired product. The others are by-products, which may be waste. Atom economy tells you what percentage of the mass of the starting materials ends up in the desired product, according to the balanced equation. A high atom economy is important for sustainable development and for economic reasons, because fewer resources are wasted and there is less waste to deal with.

Atom economy = (Mr of desired product from equation ÷ sum of Mr of all reactants from equation) × 100. You must use the balanced equation and multiply each Mr by its coefficient. For example, in the thermal decomposition CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂, if calcium oxide is the desired product, atom economy = 56 ÷ 100 × 100 = 56%. The other 44% of the mass ends up as carbon dioxide.

Because mass is conserved, the total Mr of all reactants equals the total Mr of all products, so you can also divide by the total Mr of the products. Reactions with only one product, such as addition reactions like C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH, have an atom economy of 100%, because all of the atoms in the reactants end up in the desired product.

Atom economy is different from percentage yield. Atom economy is a theoretical value calculated from the equation, and tells you how much of the starting material could become the product. Percentage yield is found from experiment and tells you how much product you actually got compared with the maximum possible. A reaction can have a high yield but a low atom economy, or the other way round.

Higher tier students should be able to explain why a particular reaction pathway is chosen to make a product. Chemists consider the atom economy, the percentage yield, the rate of reaction, the position of equilibrium (for reversible reactions) and the usefulness of any by-products. For example, ethanol can be made by hydrating ethene (100% atom economy, fast, continuous, but uses a non-renewable raw material from crude oil) or by fermenting sugar (51% atom economy, slow, but uses renewable crops and the carbon dioxide by-product can be sold). A low atom economy matters less if the by-product can be sold or used.
keyFacts: Atom economy measures the percentage of starting materials that end up as useful products.
Atom economy = (Mr of desired product ÷ sum of Mr of all reactants) × 100, using the balanced equation.
Multiply each Mr by its coefficient in the balanced equation.
Reactions with only one product have 100% atom economy.
A high atom economy is important for sustainable development and for economic reasons.
Low atom economy means more waste products and more raw materials used per kg of product.
Atom economy is calculated from the equation; percentage yield is found by experiment.
(HT) Choice of reaction pathway depends on atom economy, yield, rate, equilibrium position and usefulness of by-products.

keyTerms.definition: The percentage of the total mass of reactants that ends up in the desired product, calculated from the balanced equation.
The product that the reaction is carried out to make.
A product made in a reaction that is not the desired product; it may be waste or may be useful.
Meeting the needs of people today without stopping future generations from meeting their needs.
The series of reactions used to make a particular product from starting materials.
A reaction in which two or more molecules join to form a single product, giving 100% atom economy.

equations.name: Atom economy
equations.formula: percentage atom economy = (relative formula mass of desired product from equation ÷ sum of relative formula masses of all reactants from equation) × 100

workedExamples.title: Thermal decomposition
workedExamples.question: Calculate the atom economy for making calcium oxide from calcium carbonate: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. (Ar: C = 12, O = 16, Ca = 40)

workedExamples.title: Using coefficients
workedExamples.question: Iron is extracted by Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. Calculate the atom economy for making iron. (Ar: C = 12, O = 16, Fe = 56)
steps: Sum of Mr of reactants: Fe₂O₃ = 160; 3CO = 3 × 28 = 84; total = 244.
Mr of desired product from equation: 2Fe = 2 × 56 = 112.

workedExamples.title: Comparing two methods for ethanol
workedExamples.question: Compare the atom economy of making ethanol by (A) hydration: C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH and (B) fermentation: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂. (Ar: H = 1, C = 12, O = 16)
steps: A: reactants 28 + 18 = 46; product C₂H₅OH = 46. Atom economy = 46 ÷ 46 × 100 = 100%.
B: reactant C₆H₁₂O₆ = 180; desired product 2C₂H₅OH = 2 × 46 = 92. Atom economy = 92 ÷ 180 × 100 = 51.1%.
Hydration has the higher atom economy because ethanol is the only product.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often forget to multiply Mr values by the coefficients in the equation.
misconceptions.right: In fact atom economy uses the masses shown in the balanced equation, so 2Fe counts as 2 × 56 = 112.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think atom economy and percentage yield are the same thing.
misconceptions.right: In fact atom economy is calculated from the equation and is about wasted atoms in by-products; percentage yield is measured in experiments and is about how much of the possible product was actually collected.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often divide by the Mr of the reactant they think is most important, rather than all reactants.
misconceptions.right: In fact you must divide by the sum of the Mr values of all the reactants (which equals the sum of all the products).

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the reaction with the highest atom economy is always the one chosen.
misconceptions.right: In fact chemists also consider yield, rate, equilibrium position, cost and availability of raw materials and whether by-products can be sold or used.

realWorld: Green chemistry aims for reactions with high atom economy; many modern medicines are now made by routes that waste far fewer atoms than older methods.
Ethanol is made both by fermentation (lower atom economy, renewable sugar) and by hydration of ethene (100% atom economy, non-renewable crude oil), and the choice depends on local resources.
In lime production, the carbon dioxide by-product from heating limestone can be captured and sold, for example for fizzy drinks, which reduces waste.
higherTier: Explain why a particular reaction pathway is chosen to produce a specified product given appropriate data such as atom economy (if not calculated), yield, rate, equilibrium position and usefulness of by-products.
separateOnlyContent: The whole of this subtopic (atom economy) is in separate Chemistry only, not Combined Science Trilogy.
examTips: Write the equation out and put Mr × coefficient under each formula before calculating.
Check: total Mr of reactants should equal total Mr of products; if not, recheck your Mr values.
If there is only one product, the atom economy is 100% and you can say so without a long calculation.
In evaluation questions, discuss more than one factor: atom economy, yield, rate, equilibrium, raw materials and by-products.
Give answers to 3 significant figures unless asked otherwise.
summary: Atom economy shows how much of the reactants ends up as the desired product.
Atom economy = Mr of desired product ÷ total Mr of reactants × 100.
Use coefficients from the balanced equation.
High atom economy is good for sustainability and profits.
(HT) Pathway choice also depends on yield, rate, equilibrium and by-products.

questions.question: What does atom economy measure?
options: How fast a reaction happens
The amount of starting materials that end up as useful products
The mass of product actually collected
The energy released by a reaction
markScheme: 1 mark: the amount of starting materials that end up as useful products
questions.explanation: Atom economy shows what percentage of the reactants' mass ends up in the desired product. The mass actually collected relates to yield.

questions.question: What is the atom economy of the reaction C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH?
questions.explanation: There is only one product, so all of the reactant atoms end up in it.

questions.question: Why is a high atom economy important?
options: It makes the reaction faster
It always gives a 100% yield
It means the reaction is reversible
It means less waste and is better for sustainability
markScheme: 1 mark: it means less waste and is better for sustainability
questions.explanation: A high atom economy means more of the raw materials end up in the product, so fewer resources are used and less waste is made. It does not affect the rate or guarantee the yield.

questions.question: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. What is the atom economy for producing calcium oxide? (Ar: C = 12, O = 16, Ca = 40)
questions.explanation: 56 ÷ 100 × 100 = 56%. 44% would be the atom economy if carbon dioxide were the desired product.

questions.question: Which type of reaction always has an atom economy of 100%?
options: A thermal decomposition
A reaction with only one product
A neutralisation reaction
A displacement reaction
markScheme: 1 mark: a reaction with only one product
questions.explanation: With only one product, nothing is wasted as a by-product. Decompositions, neutralisations and displacements usually produce more than one product.

questions.question: 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂. What is the atom economy for producing hydrogen? (Ar: H = 1, O = 16)
questions.explanation: Desired product 2H₂ = 4; reactants 2H₂O = 36. 4 ÷ 36 × 100 = 11.1%. 5.6% forgets the coefficient 2 on H₂ only.

questions.question: Which statement about atom economy and percentage yield is correct?
options: They are always equal
Atom economy is measured by experiment
A reaction with 100% atom economy always has a 100% yield
Atom economy is calculated from the balanced equation
markScheme: 1 mark: atom economy is calculated from the balanced equation
questions.explanation: Atom economy is theoretical. Percentage yield depends on what happens in practice, so a 100% atom economy reaction can still have a low yield (for example, if it is reversible).

questions.question: A company could make a product by route X (atom economy 90%, slow, by-product is waste) or route Y (atom economy 60%, fast, by-product can be sold). Which statement is the best evaluation?
options: Route X must be chosen because its atom economy is higher
Route Y may be chosen because its rate is higher and its by-product is useful
Route Y must be chosen because all fast reactions are better
The two routes are equally good
markScheme: 1 mark: route Y may be chosen because its rate is higher and its by-product is useful
questions.explanation: Atom economy is only one factor. A useful by-product reduces waste in practice, and a faster rate increases output.

questions.question: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂. What is the atom economy for producing hydrogen? (Ar: H = 1, Cl = 35.5, Zn = 65)
questions.explanation: Reactants: 65 + 2 × 36.5 = 138. Desired product H₂ = 2. 2 ÷ 138 × 100 = 1.449...%, which is 1.4% to 2 significant figures (not 1.5%, because 1.449 rounds down). 98.6% is the atom economy for zinc chloride.

questions.question: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. Calculate the atom economy for making calcium oxide. (Ar: C = 12, O = 16, Ca = 40)
questions.explanation: Mr of CaO = 56 and Mr of CaCO₃ = 100, so atom economy = 56%.

questions.question: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. Calculate the atom economy for making ammonia. (Ar: H = 1, N = 14)
questions.explanation: Ammonia is the only product: 34 ÷ 34 × 100 = 100%.

questions.question: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. Calculate the atom economy for making iron. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (Ar: C = 12, O = 16, Fe = 56)
questions.explanation: Remember to multiply by coefficients. Over half the mass of the reactants ends up as carbon dioxide.

questions.question: 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂. Calculate the atom economy for producing hydrogen by electrolysis of water. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (Ar: H = 1, O = 16)
questions.explanation: 4 ÷ 36 × 100 = 11.1%. Most of the mass ends up as oxygen, which could be a useful by-product.

questions.question: Ethanol can be made by fermentation: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂. Calculate the atom economy for making ethanol. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (Ar: H = 1, C = 12, O = 16)
questions.explanation: Two molecules of ethanol (Mr 46) form for each glucose molecule, so the desired mass is 92.

questions.question: Hydrogen can be made from methane: CH₄ + H₂O → CO + 3H₂. Calculate the atom economy for making hydrogen. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (Ar: H = 1, C = 12, O = 16)
questions.explanation: Hydrogen atoms are very light, so even though three molecules form, they make up only 17.6% of the mass.

questions.question: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂. Calculate the atom economy for making zinc chloride. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (Ar: H = 1, Cl = 35.5, Zn = 65)
questions.explanation: Only the light hydrogen is wasted, so the atom economy for zinc chloride is very high.

questions.question: Titanium is extracted by TiCl₄ + 4Na → Ti + 4NaCl. Calculate the atom economy for making titanium. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (Ar: Na = 23, Cl = 35.5, Ti = 48)
questions.explanation: Most of the mass ends up as sodium chloride, so the atom economy for titanium is only 17.0%, one reason titanium is expensive.

questions.question: Write the equation for calculating percentage atom economy.
acceptedAnswers: Mr of desired product ÷ sum of Mr of all reactants × 100
relative formula mass of desired product divided by total relative formula mass of reactants times 100
markScheme: 1 mark: (Mr of desired product from equation ÷ sum of Mr of all reactants from equation) × 100
questions.explanation: This must be recalled. Use values from the balanced equation, including coefficients.

questions.question: State what is meant by a by-product.
markScheme: 1 mark: a product of a reaction that is not the desired (wanted) product
questions.explanation: By-products lower the atom economy, unless they can be used.

questions.question: Give two reasons why chemical companies want reactions with a high atom economy.
markScheme: 1 mark: less waste produced / fewer resources used (sustainable development)
1 mark: lower costs / more profit (economic reasons)
questions.explanation: The specification gives both sustainability and economic reasons.

questions.question: Explain the difference between atom economy and percentage yield.
markScheme: 1 mark: atom economy is calculated from the balanced equation and shows the fraction of reactant mass that ends up in the desired product
1 mark: percentage yield compares the mass of product actually made with the maximum theoretical mass
questions.explanation: One is about atoms lost to by-products in theory; the other is about product lost or not formed in practice.

questions.question: A reaction has an atom economy of 100% but a percentage yield of 40%. Suggest an explanation.
markScheme: 1 mark: 100% atom economy because there is only one product (no by-products)
1 mark: low yield because the reaction is reversible / does not go to completion / product is lost in separation
questions.explanation: Atom economy and yield are independent: an addition reaction that reaches equilibrium can have both values described.

questions.question: Compare the atom economy of making ethanol by hydration of ethene (C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH) and by fermentation (C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂). (Ar: H = 1, C = 12, O = 16)
markScheme: 1 mark: hydration has the higher atom economy because ethanol is the only product
questions.explanation: Fermentation loses almost half the mass of glucose as carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Lime (calcium oxide) is made by heating limestone, which has an atom economy of 56%. Suggest how the company could make the process more sustainable without changing the reaction.
markScheme: 1 mark: capture the carbon dioxide by-product
1 mark: and sell or use it (for example in fizzy drinks or greenhouses), so it is not wasted or released
questions.explanation: If a by-product is useful, the overall waste falls even though the calculated atom economy is unchanged.

questions.question: State the atom economy of any reaction that has only one product.
questions.explanation: All of the reactant atoms end up in the single product, so nothing is wasted.

questions.question:
Copper can be extracted from copper oxide in two ways:
Method 1: 2CuO + C → 2Cu + CO₂
Method 2: CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O
Calculate the atom economy of each method and state which is better in terms of atom economy. (Ar: H = 1, C = 12, O = 16, Cu = 63.5)
markScheme: Indicative content: Method 1: reactants = (2 × 79.5) + 12 = 171; product 2Cu = 127; 127 ÷ 171 × 100 = 74.3%. Method 2: reactants = 79.5 + 2 = 81.5; product Cu = 63.5; 63.5 ÷ 81.5 × 100 = 77.9%. Method 2 has the higher atom economy; its by-product, water, is harmless, while method 1 releases carbon dioxide.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): both atom economies correct with working, and the correct method identified.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one atom economy correct, or a correct method with errors.
questions.explanation: Method 1 is 74.3% and method 2 is 77.9%, so method 2 is slightly better by atom economy, and its by-product is water rather than carbon dioxide.

questions.question:
Ethanol can be made by two methods.
Hydration of ethene: C₂H₄ + H₂O ⇌ C₂H₅OH; atom economy 100%; about 95% yield after recycling unreacted ethene; fast; continuous process at 300 °C and 60 atmospheres; ethene comes from crude oil.
Fermentation: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂; atom economy 51.1%; slow; batch process at about 30 °C; sugar comes from crops; carbon dioxide can be sold.
Evaluate the two methods and suggest which is better for a country with plenty of farmland but no oil.
markScheme: Indicative content: hydration has 100% atom economy, so no by-products; high yield; fast rate and continuous process so large output; but needs high temperature and pressure (high energy costs); raw material ethene from crude oil, which is non-renewable and would have to be imported. Fermentation has lower atom economy (51.1%) but CO₂ by-product is useful and can be sold; slow, batch process, lower output; low temperature so low energy cost; sugar is renewable; ethanol produced is impure and needs distillation. Conclusion: for a country with farmland and no oil, fermentation is likely better because raw materials are available locally and renewable, and the by-product can be used, despite lower atom economy and rate.

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a balanced evaluation of both methods, using atom economy, yield, rate, conditions, raw materials and by-products, with a justified conclusion linked to the country's situation.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): some advantages and disadvantages of both methods with a conclusion, but limited use of the data.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple points about one method, for example 'hydration has 100% atom economy so it is better'.
questions.explanation: Atom economy favours hydration, but the country's resources favour fermentation. A good answer weighs atom economy against rate, yield, energy use, renewability of raw materials and the value of by-products.
